hmmt-feb-2001-guts-01.title: Find the neighboring odd dates
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-01.body:
A date is odd if the month, day and year digits are all odd. Every year from 2000 to 3110 contains an even digit, so the next odd date after 2001 is the earliest one in year $3111$: $1/1/3111$. Before 2001, the latest odd year is $1999$, and its latest odd date is $11/19/1999$ (month $11$; days $31$ do not exist in November, $30$ has a $0$, and the largest day with only odd digits is $19$; December has a $2$).

From $11/19/1999$ to $1/1/2000$ is about one month, and from $2000$ to $3111$ is $1111$ years $=13332$ months. The total is about $13333$ months.

**Answer: 13333**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-02.title: Binary
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-02.body:
Sort the cups $c_1\le\dots\le c_7$. If $c_k>1+c_1+\dots+c_{k-1}$, the number $1+c_1+\dots+c_{k-1}$ (at most $64$) could not be made, since all cups from $c_k$ on are too big and the smaller ones sum to less. So $c_k\le1+(c_1+\dots+c_{k-1})$, which by induction gives $c_k\le2^{k-1}$ and total at most $1+2+\dots+64=127$. To make $127$ the total must be at least $127$, so $c_k=2^{k-1}$ exactly: $1,2,4,\dots,64$. The largest cup has $64$ cubes.

**Answer: 64**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-03.title: Catalan recursion
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-03.body:
Let $T_n$ be the number of triangulations of a convex $n$-gon, $T_2=1$ by convention. Fix a side; it belongs to exactly one triangle whose third vertex splits the rest into two smaller polygons, so $T_{n}=\sum_{k=3}^{n}T_{k-1}T_{n-k+2}$, giving $T_3=1,T_4=2,T_5=5,T_6=14,T_7=42$ (the Catalan numbers $C_{n-2}$).

**Answer: 42**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-04.title: Telescoping product
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-04.body:
$1-\frac1{n^2}=\frac{(n-1)(n+1)}{n\cdot n}$. The partial product up to $N$ is $\prod_{n=2}^N\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\prod_{n=2}^N\frac{n+1}{n}=\frac1N\cdot\frac{N+1}{2}\to\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-05.title: Euler's formula and a limiting triangle
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-05.body:
By Euler's formula $OI^2=R^2-2Rr<R^2$ (where $r>0$ is the inradius), so $IO<R$ always. Conversely, $OI^2=R^2-2Rr$ and $r\to0$ for a very flat triangle (three points on the circle very close together), so $IO\to R$. Hence the least upper bound is $R$ (not attained).

**Answer: $R$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-06.title: Complementary probability
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-06.body:
Nobody has to pass anybody exactly when each student, at the moment he leaves, is at one end of the row of students still seated. The leaving order is a uniformly random permutation. The first student to leave must be one of the $2$ end students out of $6$ (probability $\frac26$), the next must be an end student of the remaining $5$ (probability $\frac25$), then $\frac24$, $\frac23$, and the last two students are automatically fine. So $P(\text{no passing})=\frac26\cdot\frac25\cdot\frac24\cdot\frac23=\frac{2}{45}$ and the answer is $1-\frac2{45}=\frac{43}{45}$.

**Answer: $\frac{43}{45}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-07.title: Catalan numbers
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-07.body:
Let $P_n$ be the number of ways to parenthesize a product of $n$ factors. The last multiplication splits the product as (first $k$ factors)(last $n-k$ factors), so $P_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}P_kP_{n-k}$, $P_1=1$: $P_2=1,P_3=2,P_4=5,P_5=14$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-08.title: Use sums of squares and integers
Telescoping
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-08.body:
Note that $k(k+1)=\frac{k(k+1)(k+2)-(k-1)k(k+1)}{3}$. Summing for $k=1,\dots,n-1$, the right side telescopes to $\frac{(n-1)n(n+1)-0}{3}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{3}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-09.title: Factor
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-09.body:
$x^4+2x^3+2x^2+2x+1=(x+1)(x^3+x^2+x+1)$ (expand to check). Since $x^3+x^2+x+1=0$, the expression is always $0$. So the only possible value is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-10.title: Centers form an equilateral triangle around $O$
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-10.body:
Each new circle is tangent to both concentric circles, so its diameter is $R-r$ and its center is at distance $\frac{R+r}{2}$ from the common center $O$. The three centers form an equilateral triangle centered at $O$, with circumradius $\frac{R+r}2$ and side $2\cdot\frac{R-r}{2}=R-r$ (the new circles are tangent to one another). A side of an equilateral triangle is $\sqrt3$ times its circumradius, so$$R-r=\sqrt3\cdot\frac{R+r}{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ R(2-\sqrt3)=r(2+\sqrt3)\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac Rr=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{2-\sqrt3}=(2+\sqrt3)^2=7+4\sqrt3.$$

**Answer: $7+4\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-10.title: Half-angle form
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-10.body:
Let $\rho=\frac{R-r}{2}$ be the radius of the new circles and $d=\frac{R+r}2$ the distance of their centers from $O$. Two adjacent centers are $2\rho$ apart and subtend $120^\circ$ at $O$, so $\rho=d\sin60^\circ$, i.e. $\frac{R-r}{R+r}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\frac Rr=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{2-\sqrt3}=7+4\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $7+4\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-11.title: Catalan recursion
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-11.body:
Let $M_n$ be the number of non-crossing perfect matchings of $2n$ points on a circle. Point $1$ is matched to some point $2k$ (an even position, so each side has an even number of points), which splits the rest into two independent groups: $M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}M_kM_{n-1-k}$, $M_0=1$. This is the Catalan recurrence: $1,1,2,5,14,42,132$. So $M_6=132$.

**Answer: 132**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-12.title: Subtract 1 from each, then halve
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-12.body:
Writing each odd number as $2b_i+1$ with $b_i\ge0$, the condition is $\sum b_i=6$ over $8$ numbers. Sets (repetitions allowed, order irrelevant) correspond to partitions of $6$ into at most $8$ parts, and every partition of $6$ has at most $6$ parts, so the count is $p(6)=11$: $6,\ 5{+}1,\ 4{+}2,\ 4{+}1{+}1,\ 3{+}3,\ 3{+}2{+}1,\ 3{+}1{+}1{+}1,\ 2{+}2{+}2,\ 2{+}2{+}1{+}1,\ 2{+}1{+}1{+}1{+}1,\ 1^6$.

**Answer: 11**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-13.title: Calculus
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-13.body:
$f(x)=x^3-x^2-x+2$, $f'(x)=3x^2-2x-1=(3x+1)(x-1)$, with critical points $x=-\frac13$ (local max) and $x=1$ (local min). $f(1)=1>0$ and $f(-\frac13)=\frac{-1}{27}-\frac19+\frac13+2>0$, so the local minimum is positive and there is no zero for $x>-\frac13$. Since $f\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $f(-\frac13)>0$, there is exactly one zero, in $(-\infty,-\frac13)$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-14.title: Self-similarity
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-14.body:
Let $x$ be the value. The fraction starts over after one period, so the part below the $2$ is again $x$: $x=1+\cfrac{1}{1+\frac2x}=1+\dfrac{x}{x+2}$. Then $x(x+2)=(x+2)+x$, i.e. $x^2=2$, and $x>0$ gives $x=\sqrt2$ (the partial values $1,\ 1.33,\ 1.4,\dots$ approach it).

**Answer: $\sqrt2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-15.title: Ballot paths
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-15.body:
These are lattice paths that stay on or below the diagonal $y=x$, counted by the Catalan number $C_4=\frac1{5}\binom84=14$. (Direct count: $\binom84=70$ paths in all; reflecting the bad ones across $y=x+1$ gives $\binom{8}{3}=56$ bad paths, so $70-56=14$.)

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-16.title: Dyck paths
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-16.body:
These are Dyck paths with $8$ steps ($4$ up, $4$ down), counted by $C_4=14$. By the reflection principle: $\binom84-\binom83=70-56=14$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-17.title: The intended estimate
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-17.body:
The match ends essentially when Joe reaches $21$ wins; Joe wins $70\%$ of games, so on average Frank wins $\frac37\cdot21=9$ games in that time, and the match lasts $21+9=30$ games.

**Answer: 30**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-18.title: Geometric sum
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-18.body:
Let $y=x^2=-4$. The number is $-(y^5+y^4+y^3+y^2+y+1)=-\frac{y^6-1}{y-1}=-\frac{4096-1}{-5}=819=3^2\cdot7\cdot13$. The largest prime factor is $13$.

**Answer: 13**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-20.title: Impossible event
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-20.body:
If six letters are in their correct envelopes, the seventh letter must go in the one remaining envelope, which is its own. So exactly six correct is impossible: the probability is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-21.title: Differentiate a geometric series
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-21.body:
Differentiating $\frac1{1-x}=\sum_{i\ge0}x^i$ three times gives $\frac6{(1-x)^4}=\sum_{i\ge0}(i+1)(i+2)(i+3)x^i$ for $|x|<1$. At $x=-\frac12$ the sum from $i=0$ is $\frac{6}{(3/2)^4}=\frac{96}{81}=\frac{32}{27}$. The given sum starts at $i=1$, so subtract the $i=0$ term $1\cdot2\cdot3=6$: $\frac{32}{27}-6=-\frac{130}{27}$.

**Answer: $-\frac{130}{27}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-22.title: Discriminant condition
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-22.body:
If the man runs at speed $v$ from his original position, he catches the train when $vt=2t^2+d_0$, i.e. $2t^2-vt+d_0=0$ has a real root $t\ge0$. This happens iff the discriminant $v^2-8d_0\ge0$. So the smallest speed is $v=\sqrt{8d_0}$.

Requiring $v=k^2$ to be a perfect square ($k=1,2,3,\dots$) gives $8d_0=k^4$, $d_0=\frac{k^4}8$. The $n$th smallest value is $d_0=\dfrac{n^4}{8}$. (If $d_0$ must be an integer, $k$ must be even and the values are $2m^4$, so the $n$th is $2n^4$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{n^4}{8}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-23.title: Multiply independent conditions
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-23.body:
A $2$-digit number has tens digit $1$ to $9$ and ones digit $0$ to $9$, all combinations equally likely, so the tens digits and ones digits are independent. Tens digits all different: $\frac99\cdot\frac89\cdot\frac79=\frac{56}{81}$. Ones digits all different: $\frac{10}{10}\cdot\frac9{10}\cdot\frac8{10}=\frac{72}{100}$. The probability is $\frac{56}{81}\cdot\frac{72}{100}=\frac{4032}{8100}=\frac{112}{225}$.

**Answer: $\frac{112}{225}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-24.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-24.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $D=(0,1)$. A dilation with ratio $k$ gives $C'=(k,k)$. Then $BC'^2=(k-1)^2+k^2=841$, so $k^2-k-420=0$, $k=21$ (or $k=-20$). Triangle $BDC'$ has base $BD=\sqrt2$, and the distance from $C'=(k,k)$ to the line $BD$ ($x+y=1$) is $\frac{|2k-1|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{41}{\sqrt2}$ in both cases. Its area is $\frac12\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\frac{41}{\sqrt2}=\frac{41}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{41}2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-25.title: Wilson's theorem
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-25.body:
$101$ is prime, so by Wilson's theorem $100!\equiv-1\pmod{101}$. The remainder is $100$.

**Answer: 100**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-25.title: Pair inverses
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-25.body:
Modulo $101$, each $a\in\{2,\dots,99\}$ has an inverse $a^{-1}\ne a$ in the same set (only $\pm1$ are self-inverse), so these numbers pair up with product $1$. Thus $100!\equiv1\cdot100\cdot1\equiv-1\equiv100$.

**Answer: 100**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-26.title: Central angles of the tangent points
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-26.body:
Since $OP_1\perp PP_1$ and $OP$ bisects $\angle P_1PP_2$, $\angle POP_1=90^\circ-\frac{45^\circ}{2}=67.5^\circ$, so the tangent points are at $\pm67.5^\circ$ from ray $OP$. Likewise the tangent points from $Q$ are at $\pm75^\circ$ from ray $OQ$.

Take $O$ between $P$ and $Q$ (segment $PQ$ passes through $O$), so ray $OQ$ is opposite to ray $OP$. Measuring angles from ray $OP$, the $P$-points are at $\pm67.5^\circ$ and the $Q$-points at $180^\circ\pm75^\circ=105^\circ,\,255^\circ$. The nearest pair is $67.5^\circ$ and $105^\circ$ (or symmetrically $-67.5^\circ,-105^\circ$): $37.5^\circ$ apart, an arc of length $37.5^\circ\cdot\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}\cdot1=\frac{5\pi}{24}$.

(If $P,Q$ were allowed on the same side of $O$, the tangent points $67.5^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ would be only $7.5^\circ=\frac\pi{24}$ apart.)

**Answer: $\frac{5\pi}{24}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-27.title: Triangles are best
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-27.body:
All $12$ matches are used, so the polygons' perimeters $p_1,\dots,p_k$ add up to $12$ and each is at least $3$ (a polygon needs at least $3$ matches), so $k\le4$. A regular $m$-gon of perimeter $p$ has area $\frac{p^2}{4m\tan(\pi/m)}$, which increases with $m$, so for fixed perimeter the equilateral triangle has the least area, namely $\frac{\sqrt3}{36}p^2$. The total area is at least $\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\sum p_i^2\ge\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\cdot\frac{12^2}{k}\ge\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\cdot\frac{144}{4}=\sqrt3$, with equality for four equilateral triangles of side $1$ (area $4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}4=\sqrt3$).

**Answer: $\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-28.title: Count by number of black marbles
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-28.body:
Let $k$ be the number of black marbles ($0\le k\le2$); the other $4-k$ marbles are red/blue with at most $5$ red and $4$ blue. For $k=0$: $4$ marbles split as $(r,b)=(4,0),\dots,(0,4)$: $5$ ways. For $k=1$: $3$ marbles: $4$ ways. For $k=2$: $2$ marbles: $3$ ways. Total $5+4+3=12$.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-29.title: Bijection with Dyck paths
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-29.body:
Write $a_i=1-k_i$ with $k_i\ge0$ and encode the sequence as the path $UD^{k_1}UD^{k_2}\cdots UD^{k_5}$ (each $U$ raises the height by $1$, each $D$ lowers it): the height after the $i$th block is the partial sum $a_1+\dots+a_i\ge0$. Append one more $U$ and then $D^{s_5+1}$, where $s_5$ is the last partial sum, to get a Dyck path of semilength $6$. Conversely every Dyck path of semilength $6$ ends with a $UD^{j}$ block, and removing it leaves exactly such a sequence. So the count is the Catalan number $C_6=132$ (also confirmed by direct enumeration).

**Answer: 132**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-30.title: Monotonicity of $f(x)=\arctan x-x^2+1.6$
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-30.body:
$f'(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}-2x$ is positive for $x\le0$ and has exactly one zero $x_0>0$ (since $2x(1+x^2)=1$ has exactly one positive root), after which it is negative. So $f$ increases on $(-\infty,x_0)$ and decreases on $(x_0,\infty)$. Since $f(0)=1.6>0$ we get $f(x_0)>0$, and $f\to-\infty$ at both ends, so there is exactly one root on each side of $x_0$: $2$ roots (near $x\approx-0.92$ and $x\approx1.62$).

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-31.title: Count outcomes
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-31.body:
The sum is between $2$ and $12$, so it must be $5$ or $10$. Sum $5$: $(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1)$, that is $4$ ways. Sum $10$: $(4,6),(5,5),(6,4)$, that is $3$ ways. Probability $\frac{4+3}{36}=\frac7{36}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{36}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-32.title: 321-avoiding permutations
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-32.body:
These are the $321$-avoiding permutations of $7$ elements, counted by the Catalan number $C_7=\frac1{8}\binom{14}{7}=429$ (a brute-force enumeration of all $5040$ permutations confirms it).

Idea: such a permutation is a merge of two increasing subsequences, namely its left-to-right maxima and the remaining entries; the positions and values of the left-to-right maxima determine the permutation, and the admissible choices correspond to Dyck paths of semilength $7$.

**Answer: 429**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-33.title: The car moves the whole time
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-33.body:
The car always moves at twice the speed of the soldiers, until each soldier has marched $15$ miles. In the time the soldiers march $15$ miles the car drives $2\cdot15=30$ miles. (The details of the back-and-forth trips only affect where the car is at the end, by less than a mile.) So $30$ miles are added to the car.

**Answer: 30**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-34.title: Difference of roots
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-34.body:
For roots $r_1,r_2$ of $2x^2-mx-8$: $r_1+r_2=\frac m2$, $r_1r_2=-4$, so $(r_1-r_2)^2=\frac{m^2}4+16$. Setting this equal to $(m-1)^2$ gives $3m^2-8m-60=0$, so $m=6$ or $m=-\frac{10}{3}$.

Check: $m=6$: roots $4,-1$, which differ by $5=m-1$. $m=-\frac{10}3$: roots $\frac43,-3$, which differ by $\frac{13}3=|m-1|$ (equal to $m-1$ if we subtract the larger root from the smaller).

**Answer: $m=6$ or $m=-\frac{10}3$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-35.title: Factor
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-35.body:
$m^5-5m^3+4m=m(m^2-1)(m^2-4)=(m-2)(m-1)m(m+1)(m+2)$, a product of five consecutive integers, so it is divisible by $5!=120$. For $m=5$ it is $3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6\cdot7=2520=120\cdot21$, for $m=6$ it is $4\cdot5\cdot6\cdot7\cdot8=6720=120\cdot56$, and for $m=10$ it is $8\cdot9\cdot10\cdot11\cdot12=95040=120\cdot792$. Since $\gcd(21,56,792)=1$, no larger number divides all of them.

**Answer: 120**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-36.title: Catalan count
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-36.body:
Such sequences are the ballot-type sequences (equivalently lattice paths staying on one side of a diagonal). Counting by length $n$ ($a_n\in[a_{n-1},n]$) gives $1,2,5,14,42$ for $n=1,\dots,5$, the Catalan numbers. So the count for $n=5$ is $C_5=42$ (confirmed by direct enumeration).

**Answer: 42**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-37.title: Leave a multiple of 7
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-37.body:
Whoever leaves a multiple of $7$ matches for the opponent wins: whatever the opponent takes ($1$ to $6$), the player takes $7$ minus that, restoring a multiple of $7$, until $0$ remain. Since $30=28+2$, Alex takes $2$ matches first.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-38.title: Geometric probability
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-38.body:
Let the two professors arrive at times $s,t$ minutes after noon, independently and uniformly in $[0,120]$. Their $15$-minute lunches overlap iff $|s-t|<15$. The complement is two triangles with legs $105$ in the square of side $120$, so $P=1-\left(\frac{105}{120}\right)^2=1-\frac{49}{64}=\frac{15}{64}$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{64}$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-38.title: If lunches must end by 2:00
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-38.body: If each lunch must finish by $2$:00, the start times are uniform in $[0,105]$ and the probability is $1-\left(\frac{90}{105}\right)^2=\frac{13}{49}$. The official answer uses the first reading.

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-40.title: Factor 1001
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-40.body:
A number $ABC,ABC=\overline{ABC}\cdot1001=\overline{ABC}\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13$. Since the product has five prime factors, the three-digit number $\overline{ABC}$ is a product of two primes, one of which is $491$: $\overline{ABC}=491\cdot2=982$ (the only multiple of $491$ below $1000$ besides $491$ itself, which is prime). The product is $982\cdot1001=982982=2\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot491$.

**Answer: 982982**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-41.title: Multiply by the base
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-41.body:
$\left(a+\frac1a\right)^3=\left(a+\frac1a\right)^2\left(a+\frac1a\right)=3\left(a+\frac1a\right)=3a+\frac3a$. Since $a+\frac1a=\pm\sqrt3$, this equals $\pm3\sqrt3$ (real $a$ with $a+\frac1a=\sqrt3$ do not exist, since $|a+\frac1a|\ge2$ for real $a$; for complex $a$ both signs occur).

**Answer: $3\left(a+\dfrac1a\right)$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-42.title: Difference of the two radicals
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-42.body:
We need $x\ge1$. Let $u=\sqrt{x-\frac1x}$, $v=\sqrt{1-\frac1x}$, so $u+v=x$ and $u^2-v^2=x-1$. Hence $u-v=\frac{x-1}{x}=1-\frac1x$. Then $v=\frac12\left(x-1+\frac1x\right)=\frac{x^2-x+1}{2x}$, and $v^2=1-\frac1x=\frac{x-1}x$ gives $(x^2-x+1)^2=4x(x-1)$. With $y=x^2-x$: $(y+1)^2=4y$, so $(y-1)^2=0$, $y=1$, i.e. $x^2-x-1=0$ and $x=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ (the positive root, with $x\ge1$). Check: $x\approx1.618$, $\sqrt{x-1/x}=\sqrt{1}=1$ and $\sqrt{1-1/x}\approx0.618$, sum $1.618$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-43.title: Geometric condition
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-43.body:
Let the number be $c$. Then $(50+c)^2=(20+c)(100+c)$: $2500+100c+c^2=2000+120c+c^2$, so $c=25$. The new sequence is $45,75,125$ with ratio $a=\frac{75}{45}=\frac{125}{75}=\frac53$.

**Answer: $\frac53$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-44.title: Three similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-44.body:
The three lines cut off three small triangles at the interior point $P$, each similar to $ABC$ with ratios $x,y,z$. The small triangle with a side on $BC$ has that side equal to the middle segment: $a'=xa$; similarly $b'=yb$, $c'=zc$. The remaining pieces on side $BC$ are sides of parallelograms equal to $ya$ and $za$, so $a=a'+ya+za=(x+y+z)a$, giving $x+y+z=1$. Hence $\frac{a'}a+\frac{b'}b+\frac{c'}c=x+y+z=1$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-45.title: Count row by row
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-45.body:
A circle in the second row sits above two adjacent base circles; the $3$ gaps between the $4$ base circles are positions $1,2,3$, and each can hold a second-row circle or not. A third-row circle sits above two adjacent second-row circles. Counting by the set $S$ of occupied second-row positions: $S$ with no two adjacent positions gives only that arrangement: $\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,3\}$ ($5$ stackings). $S=\{1,2\}$ or $\{2,3\}$: the pair may carry one third-row circle or none ($2$ each, $4$ total). $S=\{1,2,3\}$: the third row can hold a subset of its two positions, and if both are present a fourth-row circle may sit above them: $\emptyset,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\},\{a,b\}+$top, that is $5$. Total $5+4+5=14$, the Catalan number $C_4$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-46.title: Structure of the figure
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-46.body:
At stage $k$ ($k=1,2,\dots$) the current lower-right rectangle is split into four; call its upper-left, upper-right and lower-left parts $A_k,B_k,C_k$, and the lower-right part is split further at stage $k+1$.

**Edge-sharing ($n$).** $A_k$ shares an edge with $B_k$ and $C_k$; $B_k$ shares edges with $A_{k+1}$ and $B_{k+1}$; $C_k$ with $A_{k+1}$ and $C_{k+1}$. Since $B_k,A_{k+1},B_{k+1}$ are pairwise edge-adjacent, $n\ge3$. Three colors suffice: color $A_k$ with $1$ for all $k$ and give $B_k,C_k$ color $2$ for odd $k$ and $3$ for even $k$ (check: $B_k\ne A_{k+1}$ and $B_k\neq B_{k+1}$, $A_k\ne B_k$). So $n=3$.

**Corner-sharing ($m$).** At the center of the stage-$k$ rectangle, the four rectangles $A_k,B_k,C_k,A_{k+1}$ all meet, so $m\ge4$. Four colors suffice: if stage $k$ uses $(A_k,B_k,C_k)$ colors $(a,b,c)$ with fourth color $d$, color stage $k+1$ with $(A,B,C)=(d,c,a)$. This respects all corner adjacencies ($A_{k+1}$ touches $A_k,B_k,C_k$; $B_{k+1}$ touches $B_k$ and $A_{k+1}$; $C_{k+1}$ touches $C_k$ and $A_{k+1}$). So $m=4$.

**Answer: $(3,4)$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-48.title: Euler's prime-generating polynomial
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-48.body:
For $x=1,2,\dots,39$ the values $x^2+x+41$ are all prime (Euler's polynomial; one checks them directly). For $x=40$: $40^2+40+41=1681=41^2$, composite. So the smallest such $x$ is $40$. (Indeed $x^2+x+41$ is divisible by $41$ iff $41\mid x(x+1)$, first at $x=40$, and if $x\ge1$ the value then exceeds $41$.)

**Answer: 40**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-49.title: Official key
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-49.body:
The official solution states that the numbers are written in base $15$ and that the answer is $6$. I could not reproduce this reasoning from the statement as printed.

**Answer: 6** (official)

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-50.title: Period of the last digit
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-50.body:
Modulo $2$ the sequence is $1,1,0,1,1,0,\dots$ with least period $3$. Modulo $5$ it is $1,1,2,3,0,3,3,1,4,0,4,4,3,2,0,2,2,4,1,0,1,1,\dots$: the pair $(1,1)$ first reappears after $20$ terms, so the least period is $20$. A sequence defined by a recurrence is periodic with period $t$ modulo $10$ iff it is modulo $2$ and modulo $5$, so the least period modulo $10$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(3,20)=60$.

**Answer: 60**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-51.title: Project onto the floor
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-51.body:
Model the pencil as a segment. Seen from above, the hall is an $L$-wide corridor with a $90^\circ$ turn, and a segment can be carried around the corner only if its horizontal projection has length at most $2\sqrt2L$ (the classic ladder problem: at $45^\circ$ the longest segment touching the inner corner has length $2\sqrt2L$, and this is the minimum over all angles). Vertically the pencil can rise at most $L$ between the floor and the ceiling. So the length is at most $\sqrt{(2\sqrt2L)^2+L^2}=3L$.

This is attainable: tilt the pencil so its ends are at the floor and the ceiling and its horizontal projection has length exactly $2\sqrt2L$; the horizontal projection can be moved around the turn, and the height stays between $0$ and $L$.

**Answer: $3L$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-52.title: Parity of the exponent of 3
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-52.body:
$231=3\cdot7\cdot11$ and $130=2\cdot5\cdot13$. If $(m,n)\ne(0,0)$ then both are nonzero. The exponent of $3$ in $231m^2$ is $1+2v_3(m)$, which is odd, while the exponent of $3$ in $130n^2$ is $2v_3(n)$, which is even. They cannot be equal, so there are no nonzero solutions. The only solution is $(0,0)$.

**Answer: $(0,0)$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-53.title: Simplify the general term
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-53.body:
The $k$th term is $\dfrac{1}{(2k+1)^2-(2k-1)^2}\left(\dfrac1{(2k-1)^2}-\dfrac1{(2k+1)^2}\right)$. Since $\frac1{(2k-1)^2}-\frac1{(2k+1)^2}=\frac{(2k+1)^2-(2k-1)^2}{(2k-1)^2(2k+1)^2}$, the term equals $\dfrac1{(2k-1)^2(2k+1)^2}$.

Now $\frac1{(2k-1)(2k+1)}=\frac12\left(\frac1{2k-1}-\frac1{2k+1}\right)$, so$$\frac1{(2k-1)^2(2k+1)^2}=\frac14\left(\frac1{(2k-1)^2}+\frac1{(2k+1)^2}\right)-\frac14\left(\frac1{2k-1}-\frac1{2k+1}\right).$$Sum over $k\ge1$ using $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(2k-1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$ (so $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(2k+1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8-1$) and the telescoping sum $\sum_{k\ge1}\left(\frac1{2k-1}-\frac1{2k+1}\right)=1$:$$\frac14\left(\frac{\pi^2}8+\frac{\pi^2}8-1\right)-\frac14=\frac{\pi^2}{16}-\frac12\approx0.11685.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi^2}{16}-\dfrac12$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-54.title: Catalan arrangement
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-54.body:
The hyperplanes $x_i-x_j=0,\pm1$ ($i<j$) form the Catalan arrangement of type $A_3$, which has $n!\,C_n=24\cdot14$ regions for $n=4$ variables (Athanasiadis). By symmetry under permuting coordinates, each of the $4!$ cones $x_{\sigma(1)}>\dots>x_{\sigma(4)}$ contains the same number of regions, namely $C_4=14$. (A computer count of the sign patterns of $x_i-x_j-1$ inside the cone also gives $14$.)

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-55.title: Squares of multiples of 7
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-55.body:
A square is divisible by the prime $7$ iff its root is, so we count $k=7j$ with $10^6\le k^2\le10^9$, i.e. $1000\le k\le\lfloor\sqrt{10^9}\rfloor=31622$. The multiples of $7$ in this range number $\lfloor31622/7\rfloor-\lfloor999/7\rfloor=4517-142=4375$.

**Answer: 4375**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-56.title: Circumdiameter at least the longest side
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-56.body:
Every side of a triangle is a chord of its circumcircle, so the circumdiameter is at least the longest side, which is at least $925$. So the circumradius is at least $\frac{925}2$, with equality iff the side $925$ is a diameter, i.e. the triangle has a right angle opposite it: $x^2+888^2=925^2$, $x^2=67081=259^2$, $x=259$. This value is attainable, so it minimizes the area.

**Answer: 259**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-58.title: AM-GM on the intercepts
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-58.body:
Let the legs on the axes have lengths $p$ and $q$; the hypotenuse is the line $\frac Xp+\frac Yq=1$, which passes through $(x,y)$ iff $\frac xp+\frac yq=1$. By AM-GM, $1=\frac xp+\frac yq\ge2\sqrt{\frac{xy}{pq}}$, so $pq\ge4xy$ and the area $\frac{pq}2\ge2xy$, with equality when $\frac xp=\frac yq=\frac12$, i.e. $p=2x,q=2y$.

**Answer: $2xy$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-59.title: Positions where the player to move loses
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-59.body:
Label a pile size $k$ as $L$ if the player to move loses and $W$ otherwise. $0$ is $L$ (the previous player emptied the pile). A pile $k\ge1$ is $W$ if one of the two moves ($k\pm s$, $s$ the largest square $\le k$) leads to an $L$ position, and $L$ if both moves lead to $W$ positions. For example $1\to0$ is a win, so $1$ is $W$; $2\to1$ or $3$... and so on. A computer search over this recursion gives the $L$ positions below $1000$:

$5,\ 20,\ 29,\ 45,\ 80,\ 101,\ 116,\ 135,\ 145,\ 165,\ 173,\ 236,\ 257,\ 397,\ 404,\ 445,\ 477,\ 540,\ 565,\ 580,\ 585,\ 629,\ 666,\ 836,\ 845,\ 885,\ 909,\ 944,\ 949,\ 954,\ 975$.

For $n=5$ this is the example in the statement (any move leaves $1$ or $9$, from which the next player empties the pile). $n=20$: from $20$ the moves go to $4$ or $36$, both winning for the next player. Any of these values is an acceptable answer.

**Answer: e.g. $20$**

hmmt-feb-2001-guts-60.title: Check small cases
hmmt-feb-2001-guts-60.body:
Let $a_n=n!-(n-1)!+\dots\pm1!$. Then $a_1=1$, $a_2=1$ (not prime), $a_3=6-2+1=5$ (prime), $a_4=24-5+\dots$: using $a_n=n!-a_{n-1}$: $a_4=24-5=19$, $a_5=120-19=101$, $a_6=720-101=619$, $a_7=5040-619=4421$, $a_8=40320-4421=35899$, all prime. So $n=3$ works, with $a_3=5$.

The full list of valid $n\le 61$ (checked by a primality test) is $3,4,5,6,7,8,10,15,19,41,59,61$; the official key adds $105$ and $160$ (the only ones up to $335$).

**Answer: e.g. $3$**
